dataset.description: Phase 7 golden evaluation dataset for the Nexora Commerce permission-aware enterprise RAG system. Ground truth only: it is never written to by an evaluation run. Authorization expectations are NOT restated here; the runner derives them from the Phase 4 permission engine and the Phase 2 document catalog. 'expected_sources' names the authorized documents a correct answer must be grounded in; 'forbidden_sources' names the specific documents this case is probing, and the runner additionally checks the complete derived deny-list for the identity. Source-reviewed remediation v1.2; alternative-source answers are permitted with explicit attribution.

This document covers the onboarding of GreenCart Organics Pvt. Ltd. (S003), a subscription-first organic grocery business, and records the closure position handed to the account team. GreenCart was the first perishable-category seller onboarded on the platform, so several standard onboarding assumptions had to be varied.
2. What Made This Onboarding Different
Three characteristics separated GreenCart from previous onboardings.
Perishable goods. A missed delivery slot is a write-off, not a reschedule. Standard dispatch SLA definitions,
which assume a failed delivery can be retried the next day, do not hold. Fulfilment requirements were therefore expressed against delivery slots rather than against dispatch windows.
Subscription ordering. GreenCart's customers buy a recurring weekly basket. Orders arrive in predictable batches tied to slot cut-offs rather than being distributed through the day. Capacity planning is concentrated rather than smooth, and a failure at a slot cut-off affects an entire cohort at once.
Connector-based integration. GreenCart runs its storefront on Shopify and did not have the engineering capacity to build a direct integration. This document records the onboarding of StrideOne Footwear Pvt. Ltd. (S004) and the delivery of its dropship integration. StrideOne holds no inventory of its own; orders are routed to third-party logistics partners who hold brand stock. 2. The Dropship Model
In a conventional marketplace integration the seller owns stock, knows where it is, and dispatches it.
StrideOne owns none of these things.
 Stock is held by four third-party logistics partners, each with its own systems and its own view of availability.

 Returns are received by the partner, so return reason data flows back through the partner rather than from StrideOne.

1. Scope of These Notes
These notes describe how GreenCart Organics (S003) is technically integrated with the platform, and record the behaviour of the integration during the two production incidents on this account in 2026. They are written for engineers who need to reason about where a fault lies when GreenCart reports a problem.
The central point is that GreenCart's integration has three layers, and most confusion on this account comes from attributing a fault to the wrong one.
Layer
Owned by
Typical failure signature

GreenCart

Connector bridge
Platform, shared operation

Nexora platform services
Platform

duplication
2. Order Intake Path
An order placed on the marketplace is delivered to the connector by webhook. The connector translates it into a Shopify order object, applies the delivery slot as a line-item property, and acknowledges. GreenCart's dark store systems read from Shopify.
Important characteristics:
 Delivery is at-least-once. The connector deduplicates on the platform order identifier before creating a Shopify order.
 Slot metadata travels as a line-item property, not as an order-level field.
This was a Shopify modelling constraint and is the reason the pilot found an amendment defect in August
2025.
 Acknowledgement is fast and processing is asynchronous, so a slow Shopify
API does not cause webhook retries at the platform end.
3. Inventory Path
Stock is maintained per dark store. The connector publishes availability at slot granularity: a SKU can be available for tomorrow's morning slot and unavailable for tonight's, because stock is allocated against slot capacity rather than against a single pool.

Root Cause as Reported Back to Support
Engineering found that the deduplication key used by the settlement ledger no longer included the order identifier for reversal entries. The key was changed during the v1.8 to v1.9 schema migration. When the batch was reprocessed after a transient job failure, the ledger treated each reversal as a new entry rather than as an existing one, so every reversal was deducted a second time.
Full technical detail is in INC-2026-0312.
Resolution
The deduplication key was corrected to include order identifier plus entry type. The affected batch was reprocessed, Operations verified the corrected payout against the Payment Recovery Runbook
(OPS-RB-004), and INR 4,82,000 was credited on 14 March 2026. The applicable rule is the platform's accountability for the accuracy of a computed settlement under the Payment and Settlement Policy

The near-exclusive concentration on S003 was the first thing I checked and the first thing I reported. It was not because the defect was account-specific. It was because GreenCart's refund-on-report category exception means this account generates far more refund events per order than any other seller, so a defect in refund processing surfaces here first.
Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 17:48 IST. The pattern - exactly two applications of the same refund, within a narrow window, concentrated on the account with the highest refund event volume - pointed at event redelivery rather than at a calculation error, and I said so in the escalation note.
Operations was included because any recovery from a seller settlement needs an operations decision, not a support decision.
Cause
The refund webhook consumer restarted during a deployment at 21:12 on 2 September. The broker redelivered events that had been processed but not acknowledged. The consumer applied refunds without checking an idempotency key, so each redelivered event produced a second refund.
Detail is in INC-2026-0903.
The Recovery Question
This was the substance of the ticket, more than the technical cause.
Operations decided that the excess INR 1,18,000 would be recovered across four settlement cycles rather than in a single deduction, and that no interest or fee would apply. The reasoning was that the seller did not cause the error and a single large debit on a cash-constrained account would have caused real operational harm for no benefit to the platform.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. The duplicated amounts were reversed at the payment-processor level where the transaction had not yet settled, which covered 412 of the
640 cases. For the remaining 228, the amount was written off rather than pursued, on cost and proportionality grounds.

Cause

Root Cause as Reported Back to Support
Engineering found that the deduplication key used by the settlement ledger no longer included the order identifier for reversal entries. The key was changed during the v1.8 to v1.9 schema migration. When the batch was reprocessed after a transient job failure, the ledger treated each reversal as a new entry rather than as an existing one, so every reversal was deducted a second time.
Full technical detail is in INC-2026-0312.
Resolution
The deduplication key was corrected to include order identifier plus entry type. The affected batch was reprocessed, Operations verified the corrected payout against the Payment Recovery Runbook
(OPS-RB-004), and INR 4,82,000 was credited on 14 March 2026. The applicable rule is the platform's accountability for the accuracy of a computed settlement under the Payment and Settlement Policy

The near-exclusive concentration on S003 was the first thing I checked and the first thing I reported. It was not because the defect was account-specific. It was because GreenCart's refund-on-report category exception means this account generates far more refund events per order than any other seller, so a defect in refund processing surfaces here first.

Escalated to Engineering at 17:48 IST. The pattern - exactly two applications of the same refund, within a narrow window, concentrated on the account with the highest refund event volume - pointed at event redelivery rather than at a calculation error, and I said so in the escalation note.
Operations was included because any recovery from a seller settlement needs an operations decision, not a support decision.
Cause
The refund webhook consumer restarted during a deployment at 21:12 on 2 September. The broker redelivered events that had been processed but not acknowledged. The consumer applied refunds without checking an idempotency key, so each redelivered event produced a second refund.
Detail is in INC-2026-0903.
The Recovery Question
This was the substance of the ticket, more than the technical cause.
Operations decided that the excess INR 1,18,000 would be recovered across four settlement cycles rather than in a single deduction, and that no interest or fee would apply. The reasoning was that the seller did not cause the error and a single large debit on a cash-constrained account would have caused real operational harm for no benefit to the platform.
Customers who received a duplicate refund were not asked to return it. The duplicated amounts were reversed at the payment-processor level where the transaction had not yet settled, which covered 412 of the
640 cases. For the remaining 228, the amount was written off rather than pursued, on cost and proportionality grounds.

She also noted something useful: buyers who retried immediately sometimes succeeded. That intermittency was the most important clue in the ticket.
First-Line Assessment
I reproduced the failure on the third attempt using a test cart against an Aurelia listing. Two attempts succeeded, one failed with the reported error.
I then checked whether the failure was specific to this seller. It was not: the same intermittent pattern appeared against a test cart on a different seller's listing. That immediately changed the character of the ticket. This was raised by S001 but it was not an S001 problem.

Cause
Release 4.12.0 changed the cart token cache key format but continued signing tokens with the previous key namespace. During the rolling deployment some instances issued tokens in the new format while others validated against the old namespace, so a buyer whose requests landed on mismatched instances saw a token validation failure. That is why retrying sometimes worked: a retry could land on a consistent pair of instances.
Impact on This Account
1,470 checkouts failed platform-wide during the 116-minute window. Aurelia's share was 312 failed checkouts. Of those, 244 buyers completed a purchase later the same day. The residual loss attributable to the account was estimated at 68 orders.
Aurelia was affected more visibly than its traffic share alone would suggest because it was running a pre-festive campaign that day.
Resolution and Seller Position
The release was rolled back within 34 minutes of detection and re-released as 4.12.1 with a version compatibility guard the following day.
On the 13 August call Ritika accepted the explanation without dispute. Her only request was notification: she wanted to know that a platform incident was in progress rather than discovering it from her own customer complaints. Report
Ritika called rather than raising a portal ticket, which on this account signals urgency. She reported that
Aurelia's customer service inbox had received eleven complaints within an hour from buyers who could not complete payment. The error message quoted by buyers was "invalid cart token, please refresh".
She also noted something useful: buyers who retried immediately sometimes succeeded. That intermittency was the most important clue in the ticket.
First-Line Assessment
I reproduced the failure on the third attempt using a test cart against an Aurelia listing. Two attempts succeeded, one failed with the reported error.
I then checked whether the failure was specific to this seller. It was not: the same intermittent pattern appeared against a test cart on a different seller's listing. That immediately changed the character of the ticket. This was raised by S001 but it was not an S001 problem.
Order placement metrics showed roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions failing platform-wide,
starting at approximately 10:40 IST.
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL
TKT-2026-0812-308 | Support Ticket
Synthetic enterprise dataset - not real data
Page 1 of 2

Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 11:44 IST, 18 minutes after the call. I marked it as a platform-wide issue affecting multiple sellers rather than a seller-specific defect, and noted the 10:40 start time. Engineering correlated that with the release of Checkout Service 4.12.0 and opened INC-2026-0812.
Timeline
Time (IST)
Event
12 Aug 10:40
Failures begin, coinciding with release 4.12.0 rollout
12 Aug 11:26

12 Aug 12:36
Rollback complete, failure rate returns to baseline
12 Aug 13:15
Support confirms successful checkouts on Aurelia listings
13 Aug 09:30
Seller call, cause and remediation explained
13 Aug 16:00
4.12.1 released with the fix
13 Aug 17:20
Ticket closed
Cause
Release 4.12.0 changed the cart token cache key format but continued signing tokens with the previous key namespace. During the rolling deployment some instances issued tokens in the new format while others validated against the old namespace, so a buyer whose requests landed on mismatched instances saw a token validation failure. That is why retrying sometimes worked: a retry could land on a consistent pair of instances.
Impact on This Account
1,470 checkouts failed platform-wide during the 116-minute window. Aurelia's share was 312 failed checkouts. Of those, 244 buyers completed a purchase later the same day. The residual loss attributable to the account was estimated at 68 orders.
Aurelia was affected more visibly than its traffic share alone would suggest because it was running a pre-festive campaign that day.
Resolution and Seller Position
The release was rolled back within 34 minutes of detection and re-released as 4.12.1 with a version compatibility guard the following day.
On the 13 August call Ritika accepted the explanation without dispute. Her only request was notification: she wanted to know that a platform incident was in progress rather than discovering it from her own customer complaints. That request was passed to Operations and is being considered as a seller status notification capability.
No compensation was requested or offered.

Issue
Aurelia's finance team was preparing its February GST filing and found that invoices for decorative lighting products listed after 1 February 2026 had been issued at 18 percent. The applicable rate for those products is 12 percent following the HSN revision.
This was raised as P2 rather than P1. Nothing was broken from a service perspective, orders were flowing normally, and no payout was blocked. But the filing deadline gave it a hard date, and an incorrect tax document is a compliance exposure for the seller rather than an inconvenience.
Scope Established
I queried invoices for the account by sub-category and rate for the February period.
Sub-category

The pattern was clean: only lighting SKUs created after the HSN revision were affected. SKUs that existed at the time of the revision had been remapped correctly. This told me the calculation logic was fine and the problem was in category mapping for new listings.
Total tax difference: INR 2,17,600.
Investigation Notes
Working with the Operations tax desk, we established that the HSN revision was applied as a one-time remap of existing SKUs. The category default for decorative lighting was left at 18 percent. Any SKU created after the remap picked up the default rather than the revised mapping.
So there was no defect in the invoicing service. The invoicing service correctly applied the rate it was given.
The mapping was incomplete.
This distinction mattered for routing. I did not escalate to Engineering, because there was nothing for
Engineering to fix in the immediate term. I routed the correction to Operations and the commercial decision to Business.
Decision Required
Support could not resolve this ticket alone. Three things had to be decided: whether to re-issue invoices or adjust prospectively, who absorbs the INR 2,17,600 difference, and whether a control should be added.
Those decisions sat with Aditya Verma and are recorded in decision record DR-2026-011. The outcome was to re-issue credit notes, absorb the difference at platform cost, and add a mapping validation control.

2026-03-09

Resolution
Mapping corrected on 27 February. Credit notes and corrected invoices issued on 5 March. Aurelia confirmed on 9 March that its February filing position was restored. A blocking validation was deployed on 18
March that prevents publication of a listing whose tax category resolves to a category default.
Support Observation
The seller found this, not the platform. There was no reconciliation check comparing the tax rate on issued invoices against the current mapping for the product's HSN classification. That gap is now closed by the blocking validation, but only for new listings. A future rate revision will still require an explicit remap and there

Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 11:44 IST, 18 minutes after the call. I marked it as a platform-wide issue affecting multiple sellers rather than a seller-specific defect, and noted the 10:40 start time. Engineering correlated that with the release of Checkout Service 4.12.0 and opened INC-2026-0812.

Cause
Release 4.12.0 changed the cart token cache key format but continued signing tokens with the previous key namespace. During the rolling deployment some instances issued tokens in the new format while others validated against the old namespace, so a buyer whose requests landed on mismatched instances saw a token validation failure. That is why retrying sometimes worked: a retry could land on a consistent pair of instances.
Impact on This Account
1,470 checkouts failed platform-wide during the 116-minute window. Aurelia's share was 312 failed checkouts. Of those, 244 buyers completed a purchase later the same day. The residual loss attributable to the account was estimated at 68 orders.
Aurelia was affected more visibly than its traffic share alone would suggest because it was running a pre-festive campaign that day.
Resolution and Seller Position
The release was rolled back within 34 minutes of detection and re-released as 4.12.1 with a version compatibility guard the following day.
On the 13 August call Ritika accepted the explanation without dispute. Her only request was notification: she wanted to know that a platform incident was in progress rather than discovering it from her own customer complaints. That request was passed to Operations and is being considered as a seller status notification capability.
No compensation was requested or offered.

for their full scope; absence from selected passages is not such support.

Report
Ritika called rather than raising a portal ticket, which on this account signals urgency. She reported that
Aurelia's customer service inbox had received eleven complaints within an hour from buyers who could not complete payment. The error message quoted by buyers was "invalid cart token, please refresh".
She also noted something useful: buyers who retried immediately sometimes succeeded. That intermittency was the most important clue in the ticket.
First-Line Assessment
I reproduced the failure on the third attempt using a test cart against an Aurelia listing. Two attempts succeeded, one failed with the reported error.
I then checked whether the failure was specific to this seller. It was not: the same intermittent pattern appeared against a test cart on a different seller's listing. That immediately changed the character of the ticket. This was raised by S001 but it was not an S001 problem.
Order placement metrics showed roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions failing platform-wide,
starting at approximately 10:40 IST.
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace

TKT-2026-0812-308 | Support Ticket

Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 11:44 IST, 18 minutes after the call. I marked it as a platform-wide issue affecting multiple sellers rather than a seller-specific defect, and noted the 10:40 start time. Engineering correlated that with the release of Checkout Service 4.12.0 and opened INC-2026-0812.
Timeline
Time (IST)
Event

Failures begin, coinciding with release 4.12.0 rollout
12 Aug 11:26

12 Aug 13:15

13 Aug 09:30

13 Aug 16:00
4.12.1 released with the fix
13 Aug 17:20
Ticket closed
Cause
Release 4.12.0 changed the cart token cache key format but continued signing tokens with the previous key namespace. During the rolling deployment some instances issued tokens in the new format while others validated against the old namespace, so a buyer whose requests landed on mismatched instances saw a token validation failure. That is why retrying sometimes worked: a retry could land on a consistent pair of instances.
Impact on This Account
1,470 checkouts failed platform-wide during the 116-minute window. Aurelia's share was 312 failed checkouts. Of those, 244 buyers completed a purchase later the same day. The residual loss attributable to the account was estimated at 68 orders.
Aurelia was affected more visibly than its traffic share alone would suggest because it was running a pre-festive campaign that day.
Resolution and Seller Position
The release was rolled back within 34 minutes of detection and re-released as 4.12.1 with a version compatibility guard the following day.
On the 13 August call Ritika accepted the explanation without dispute. Her only request was notification: she wanted to know that a platform incident was in progress rather than discovering it from her own customer complaints. That request was passed to Operations and is being considered as a seller status notification capability.
No compensation was requested or offered.

Issue
Aurelia's finance team was preparing its February GST filing and found that invoices for decorative lighting products listed after 1 February 2026 had been issued at 18 percent. The applicable rate for those products is 12 percent following the HSN revision.
This was raised as P2 rather than P1. Nothing was broken from a service perspective, orders were flowing normally, and no payout was blocked. But the filing deadline gave it a hard date, and an incorrect tax document is a compliance exposure for the seller rather than an inconvenience.
Scope Established
I queried invoices for the account by sub-category and rate for the February period.

The pattern was clean: only lighting SKUs created after the HSN revision were affected. SKUs that existed at the time of the revision had been remapped correctly. This told me the calculation logic was fine and the problem was in category mapping for new listings.
Total tax difference: INR 2,17,600.
Investigation Notes
Working with the Operations tax desk, we established that the HSN revision was applied as a one-time remap of existing SKUs. The category default for decorative lighting was left at 18 percent. Any SKU created after the remap picked up the default rather than the revised mapping.
So there was no defect in the invoicing service. The invoicing service correctly applied the rate it was given.
The mapping was incomplete.
This distinction mattered for routing. I did not escalate to Engineering, because there was nothing for
Engineering to fix in the immediate term. I routed the correction to Operations and the commercial decision to Business.
Decision Required
Support could not resolve this ticket alone. Three things had to be decided: whether to re-issue invoices or adjust prospectively, who absorbs the INR 2,17,600 difference, and whether a control should be added.
Those decisions sat with Aditya Verma and are recorded in decision record DR-2026-011. The outcome was to re-issue credit notes, absorb the difference at platform cost, and add a mapping validation control.

Resolution
Mapping corrected on 27 February. Credit notes and corrected invoices issued on 5 March. Aurelia confirmed on 9 March that its February filing position was restored. A blocking validation was deployed on 18
March that prevents publication of a listing whose tax category resolves to a category default.

or quote the units; the application attaches their original quotations.
A unit is supported only if all its substantive claims are supported.
Headings and table headers accompany the factual text they describe. Judge the
substantive claims; Markdown layout itself is not an additional factual claim.

Use kind="unsupported" for unsupported or contradicted claims. For explicit
missing-information statements, stated assumptions, or recommendations clearly
presented as advice rather than established facts, use kind="qualified".
Do not treat a promised outcome, asserted requirement, or a factual assertion
embedded in a recommendation as qualified unless that assertion is supported.
A faithful qualified answer is grounded even if incomplete.
Do not infer completed conditions from requirements, or a final/peak figure
from an initial observation. Do not treat source inventory labels as claims.
"Only", "all", "none", and similar exhaustive claims require explicit support
for their full scope; absence from selected passages is not such support.

 "notes":"brief notes"}.

Report
Ritika called rather than raising a portal ticket, which on this account signals urgency. She reported that
Aurelia's customer service inbox had received eleven complaints within an hour from buyers who could not complete payment. The error message quoted by buyers was "invalid cart token, please refresh".
She also noted something useful: buyers who retried immediately sometimes succeeded. That intermittency was the most important clue in the ticket.
First-Line Assessment
I reproduced the failure on the third attempt using a test cart against an Aurelia listing. Two attempts succeeded, one failed with the reported error.
I then checked whether the failure was specific to this seller. It was not: the same intermittent pattern appeared against a test cart on a different seller's listing. That immediately changed the character of the ticket. This was raised by S001 but it was not an S001 problem.
Order placement metrics showed roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions failing platform-wide,
starting at approximately 10:40 IST.

Escalation
Escalated to Engineering at 11:44 IST, 18 minutes after the call. I marked it as a platform-wide issue affecting multiple sellers rather than a seller-specific defect, and noted the 10:40 start time. Engineering correlated that with the release of Checkout Service 4.12.0 and opened INC-2026-0812.

Cause
Release 4.12.0 changed the cart token cache key format but continued signing tokens with the previous key namespace. During the rolling deployment some instances issued tokens in the new format while others validated against the old namespace, so a buyer whose requests landed on mismatched instances saw a token validation failure. That is why retrying sometimes worked: a retry could land on a consistent pair of instances.
Impact on This Account
1,470 checkouts failed platform-wide during the 116-minute window. Aurelia's share was 312 failed checkouts. Of those, 244 buyers completed a purchase later the same day. The residual loss attributable to the account was estimated at 68 orders.
Aurelia was affected more visibly than its traffic share alone would suggest because it was running a pre-festive campaign that day.
Resolution and Seller Position
The release was rolled back within 34 minutes of detection and re-released as 4.12.1 with a version compatibility guard the following day.
On the 13 August call Ritika accepted the explanation without dispute. Her only request was notification: she wanted to know that a platform incident was in progress rather than discovering it from her own customer complaints. That request was passed to Operations and is being considered as a seller status notification capability.
No compensation was requested or offered.

This was raised as P2 rather than P1. Nothing was broken from a service perspective, orders were flowing normally, and no payout was blocked. But the filing deadline gave it a hard date, and an incorrect tax document is a compliance exposure for the seller rather than an inconvenience.

Total tax difference: INR 2,17,600.
Investigation Notes
Working with the Operations tax desk, we established that the HSN revision was applied as a one-time remap of existing SKUs. The category default for decorative lighting was left at 18 percent. Any SKU created after the remap picked up the default rather than the revised mapping.
So there was no defect in the invoicing service. The invoicing service correctly applied the rate it was given.
The mapping was incomplete.
This distinction mattered for routing. I did not escalate to Engineering, because there was nothing for
Engineering to fix in the immediate term. I routed the correction to Operations and the commercial decision to Business.
Decision Required
Support could not resolve this ticket alone. Three things had to be decided: whether to re-issue invoices or adjust prospectively, who absorbs the INR 2,17,600 difference, and whether a control should be added.
Those decisions sat with Aditya Verma and are recorded in decision record DR-2026-011. The outcome was to re-issue credit notes, absorb the difference at platform cost, and add a mapping validation control.

results.answer:
**Activation conditions (section 4)**  
A seller may not be activated unless **all** of the following conditions are satisfied:

- **A‑1** – Commercial agreement signed and countersigned (Business)  
- **A‑2** – KYC and entity verification complete (Operations)  
- **A‑3** – Category‑specific compliance verified where applicable (Operations)  
- **A‑4** – Category and commission mapping agreed (Business)  
- **A‑5** – Named seller counterpart recorded (Business)  
- **A‑6** – Integration method selected with recorded rationale (Engineering)  
- **A‑7** – Sandbox authentication demonstrated (Engineering)  
- **A‑8** – Catalogue validation completed; failing records withheld (Operations)  
- **A‑9** – Tax category mapping resolves explicitly for every listing (Operations)  
- **A‑10** – Fulfilment nodes or logistics partners verified (Operations)  
- **A‑11** – Label generation failover tested live (Operations)  
- **A‑12** – Pilot completed with findings recorded (Operations)  
- **A‑13** – Support queue readiness confirmed (Support)

*All conditions are cumulative (R‑1) and each must be evidenced according to the closure standard (section 6); none may be satisfied by mere assertion.*

1. Purpose
This policy defines the conditions a seller must satisfy before being activated on Nexora Marketplace, the readiness conditions attached to commercial entitlements, and the mechanism by which an exception to those conditions may be granted.
It exists to ensure that commercial commitments made to a seller are supported by the seller's actual operational and technical readiness, and that any departure from that principle is deliberate, bounded and owned.
2. Scope
Applies to all new seller accounts and to any material change of integration method on an existing account.
Applies to changes in settlement frequency, tier and commercial terms on an existing account, insofar as those changes carry readiness conditions.
Does not apply to catalogue expansion, pricing changes or routine operational changes on an already-active account.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Activation
The point at which a seller's listings become buyable
Readiness condition
A verifiable condition attached to a commercial entitlement
Milestone
A readiness condition with a defined validator and date
Compensating control
A measure that bounds risk where a condition is unmet
Policy exception
A documented, time-bound departure from a stated condition
Closure standard
The evidence required to consider a condition satisfied
Two-stage onboarding
Activation on an interim process with a committed migration
4. Activation Conditions
A seller may not be activated unless all of the following are satisfied.

R-1. Conditions A-1 through A-13 are cumulative. None may be satisfied by assertion; each requires evidence meeting the closure standard in section 6.
R-2. Category compliance under A-3 must be on file before catalogue preparation begins, not before activation.
R-3. Where catalogue records fail validation, withholding the record is preferred to publishing it with poor data. Catalogue size is not an activation criterion.
5. Readiness Conditions for Commercial Entitlements
Certain commercial entitlements carry readiness conditions independent of tier.

Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: INTERNAL
POL-BIZ-003 | Policy
Page 2 of 5

R-5. Any settlement dispute resets W-1 to zero.
The seller portal describes weekly settlement as a tier feature without stating these conditions. That discrepancy was raised in January 2026 and is a known documentation gap on the seller-facing side. Until it is corrected, account managers should state the conditions explicitly when a seller raises the subject.
5.2 Tier Upgrade
R-6. Tier is reviewed annually, or on milestone completion where a conditional upgrade is in effect.
R-7. Tier may be reviewed downward where order defect rate exceeds the tier threshold for two consecutive months.
R-8. Tier and settlement frequency are separable. A tier upgrade may be granted where a settlement frequency change may not, because the two carry different and asymmetric risks: a tier change is commercially reversible at the next review, whereas settlement frequency determines how much unreconciled value is paid out before a dispute could surface.
6. Closure Standard
R-9. A condition is satisfied by evidence that the thing works, not by evidence that it has been configured.
Condition type
Acceptable evidence
Failover configuration
A successful live failover test
Monitoring or alerting
The alert observed firing in a controlled test
Data quality rule
A rejection report showing the rule acting
Interim process removal
The interim process confirmed retired
Seller-side capability
Confirmation from the named seller counterpart
Reconciliation capability
A reconciliation run compared against platform figures
R-10. A configuration entry, a ticket marked complete, or a verbal assurance is not acceptable closure evidence for any condition in section 4 or 5.
Rule R-9 was added in July 2026. A failover condition had been closed in October 2025 on a configuration entry; when the failover was required eight months later, the stored credentials had expired and no label could be generated for 2,100 perishable orders. The condition had been recorded as met and had never been true.
7. Exceptions
R-11. An exception to any condition in sections 4 or 5 requires all of the following:
1. A written rationale stating what is being waived and why.
2. A named approver with authority for the affected domain.
3. A compensating control that bounds the resulting risk.
4. Milestones with named validators where the condition is deferred rather than waived.
5. An expiry date, after which the exception lapses and the entitlement is withdrawn.
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: INTERNAL
POL-BIZ-003 | Policy
Page 3 of 5

R-12. An exception may not waive A-2 (KYC), A-3 (category compliance) or A-9 (tax mapping). These are compliance conditions, not commercial ones.
R-13. Two-stage onboarding is permitted where an interim process is used at activation, provided the exception carries an explicit exit date. An open-ended commitment to migrate is not an acceptable exception; in practice it becomes permanent.
R-14. A compensating control must be proportionate to the exposure it bounds, and must be sized against the risk rather than against the seller's convenience. A security deposit, for example, is sized against the largest single-cycle dispute observed on comparable accounts.
R-15. Every active exception is reviewed at each quarterly account review.
7.1 Worked Example
A grocery seller requested a tier upgrade and weekly settlement in January 2026, having completed four settlement cycles, with no automated reconciliation and an untested failover.
The tier upgrade was granted immediately, because tier risk is commercially reversible. Weekly settlement was deferred and tied to validation of the reconciliation milestone, with a security deposit as the compensating control and an expiry date of 31 January 2027.
Three of four milestones were subsequently met. The reconciliation milestone remains outstanding as of
September 2026, and weekly settlement has accordingly not been granted. The exception is operating as intended: the commercial benefit was delivered where it was safe to do so, and the financial control held.

R-16. Operations owns the go or no-go decision at each stage. Business owns the commercial consequences of a delay. Where these conflict, the conflict is escalated for a documented decision and is not resolved by weakening a condition.

10. Enforcement
Activation is gated in the account management system on conditions A-1 through A-13 being recorded as satisfied. Weekly settlement is gated on milestone validation.

Quarterly account reviews test every active exception. An exception past expiry with an unmet milestone results in withdrawal of the entitlement, which is a system action rather than a negotiation.

1. Purpose
This policy defines the conditions a seller must satisfy before being activated on Nexora Marketplace, the readiness conditions attached to commercial entitlements, and the mechanism by which an exception to those conditions may be granted.
It exists to ensure that commercial commitments made to a seller are supported by the seller's actual operational and technical readiness, and that any departure from that principle is deliberate, bounded and owned.
2. Scope
Applies to all new seller accounts and to any material change of integration method on an existing account.
Applies to changes in settlement frequency, tier and commercial terms on an existing account, insofar as those changes carry readiness conditions.
Does not apply to catalogue expansion, pricing changes or routine operational changes on an already-active account.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Activation
The point at which a seller's listings become buyable
Readiness condition
A verifiable condition attached to a commercial entitlement
Milestone
A readiness condition with a defined validator and date
Compensating control
A measure that bounds risk where a condition is unmet
Policy exception
A documented, time-bound departure from a stated condition
Closure standard
The evidence required to consider a condition satisfied
Two-stage onboarding
Activation on an interim process with a committed migration
4. Activation Conditions
A seller may not be activated unless all of the following are satisfied.

1. Purpose
This policy defines the conditions a seller must satisfy before being activated on Nexora Marketplace, the readiness conditions attached to commercial entitlements, and the mechanism by which an exception to those conditions may be granted.
It exists to ensure that commercial commitments made to a seller are supported by the seller's actual operational and technical readiness, and that any departure from that principle is deliberate, bounded and owned.
2. Scope
Applies to all new seller accounts and to any material change of integration method on an existing account.
Applies to changes in settlement frequency, tier and commercial terms on an existing account, insofar as those changes carry readiness conditions.
Does not apply to catalogue expansion, pricing changes or routine operational changes on an already-active account.
3. Definitions

Definition
Activation
The point at which a seller's listings become buyable
Readiness condition
A verifiable condition attached to a commercial entitlement
Milestone

Compensating control

Policy exception
A documented, time-bound departure from a stated condition
Closure standard
The evidence required to consider a condition satisfied
Two-stage onboarding
Activation on an interim process with a committed migration
4. Activation Conditions
A seller may not be activated unless all of the following are satisfied.

A seller may not be activated unless **all** of the following conditions are satisfied:

- **A‑1** – Commercial agreement signed and countersigned (Business)  
- **A‑2** – KYC and entity verification complete (Operations)  
- **A‑3** – Category‑specific compliance verified where applicable (Operations)  
- **A‑4** – Category and commission mapping agreed (Business)  
- **A‑5** – Named seller counterpart recorded (Business)  
- **A‑6** – Integration method selected with recorded rationale (Engineering)  
- **A‑7** – Sandbox authentication demonstrated (Engineering)  
- **A‑8** – Catalogue validation completed; failing records withheld (Operations)  
- **A‑9** – Tax category mapping resolves explicitly for every listing (Operations)  
- **A‑10** – Fulfilment nodes or logistics partners verified (Operations)  
- **A‑11** – Label generation failover tested live (Operations)  
- **A‑12** – Pilot completed with findings recorded (Operations)  
- **A‑13** – Support queue readiness confirmed (Support)

*All conditions are cumulative (R‑1) and each must be evidenced according to the closure standard (section 6); none may be satisfied by mere assertion.*

1. Purpose
This policy defines the conditions a seller must satisfy before being activated on Nexora Marketplace, the readiness conditions attached to commercial entitlements, and the mechanism by which an exception to those conditions may be granted.
It exists to ensure that commercial commitments made to a seller are supported by the seller's actual operational and technical readiness, and that any departure from that principle is deliberate, bounded and owned.
2. Scope
Applies to all new seller accounts and to any material change of integration method on an existing account.
Applies to changes in settlement frequency, tier and commercial terms on an existing account, insofar as those changes carry readiness conditions.
Does not apply to catalogue expansion, pricing changes or routine operational changes on an already-active account.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Activation
The point at which a seller's listings become buyable
Readiness condition
A verifiable condition attached to a commercial entitlement
Milestone
A readiness condition with a defined validator and date
Compensating control
A measure that bounds risk where a condition is unmet
Policy exception
A documented, time-bound departure from a stated condition
Closure standard
The evidence required to consider a condition satisfied
Two-stage onboarding
Activation on an interim process with a committed migration
4. Activation Conditions
A seller may not be activated unless all of the following are satisfied.

The seller portal describes weekly settlement as a tier feature without stating these conditions. That discrepancy was raised in January 2026 and is a known documentation gap on the seller-facing side. Until it is corrected, account managers should state the conditions explicitly when a seller raises the subject.
5.2 Tier Upgrade
R-6. Tier is reviewed annually, or on milestone completion where a conditional upgrade is in effect.
R-7. Tier may be reviewed downward where order defect rate exceeds the tier threshold for two consecutive months.
R-8. Tier and settlement frequency are separable. A tier upgrade may be granted where a settlement frequency change may not, because the two carry different and asymmetric risks: a tier change is commercially reversible at the next review, whereas settlement frequency determines how much unreconciled value is paid out before a dispute could surface.
6. Closure Standard
R-9. A condition is satisfied by evidence that the thing works, not by evidence that it has been configured.
Condition type
Acceptable evidence
Failover configuration
A successful live failover test
Monitoring or alerting
The alert observed firing in a controlled test
Data quality rule
A rejection report showing the rule acting
Interim process removal
The interim process confirmed retired
Seller-side capability
Confirmation from the named seller counterpart
Reconciliation capability
A reconciliation run compared against platform figures
R-10. A configuration entry, a ticket marked complete, or a verbal assurance is not acceptable closure evidence for any condition in section 4 or 5.
Rule R-9 was added in July 2026. A failover condition had been closed in October 2025 on a configuration entry; when the failover was required eight months later, the stored credentials had expired and no label could be generated for 2,100 perishable orders. The condition had been recorded as met and had never been true.
7. Exceptions
R-11. An exception to any condition in sections 4 or 5 requires all of the following:
1. A written rationale stating what is being waived and why.
2. A named approver with authority for the affected domain.
3. A compensating control that bounds the resulting risk.
4. Milestones with named validators where the condition is deferred rather than waived.
5. An expiry date, after which the exception lapses and the entitlement is withdrawn.

"},{"evidence_id":"EV-e818fdac7226","text":"R-12. An exception may not waive A-2 (KYC), A-3 (category compliance) or A-9 (tax mapping). These are compliance conditions, not commercial ones.
R-13. Two-stage onboarding is permitted where an interim process is used at activation, provided the exception carries an explicit exit date. An open-ended commitment to migrate is not an acceptable exception; in practice it becomes permanent.
R-14. A compensating control must be proportionate to the exposure it bounds, and must be sized against the risk rather than against the seller's convenience. A security deposit, for example, is sized against the largest single-cycle dispute observed on comparable accounts.
R-15. Every active exception is reviewed at each quarterly account review.
7.1 Worked Example
A grocery seller requested a tier upgrade and weekly settlement in January 2026, having completed four settlement cycles, with no automated reconciliation and an untested failover.
The tier upgrade was granted immediately, because tier risk is commercially reversible. Weekly settlement was deferred and tied to validation of the reconciliation milestone, with a security deposit as the compensating control and an expiry date of 31 January 2027.
Three of four milestones were subsequently met. The reconciliation milestone remains outstanding as of
September 2026, and weekly settlement has accordingly not been granted. The exception is operating as intended: the commercial benefit was delivered where it was safe to do so, and the financial control held.

1. Purpose
This policy defines the conditions a seller must satisfy before being activated on Nexora Marketplace, the readiness conditions attached to commercial entitlements, and the mechanism by which an exception to those conditions may be granted.
It exists to ensure that commercial commitments made to a seller are supported by the seller's actual operational and technical readiness, and that any departure from that principle is deliberate, bounded and owned.

Applies to all new seller accounts and to any material change of integration method on an existing account.

Does not apply to catalogue expansion, pricing changes or routine operational changes on an already-active account.

1. Purpose
This policy defines the conditions a seller must satisfy before being activated on Nexora Marketplace, the readiness conditions attached to commercial entitlements, and the mechanism by which an exception to those conditions may be granted.
It exists to ensure that commercial commitments made to a seller are supported by the seller's actual operational and technical readiness, and that any departure from that principle is deliberate, bounded and owned.
2. Scope
Applies to all new seller accounts and to any material change of integration method on an existing account.
Applies to changes in settlement frequency, tier and commercial terms on an existing account, insofar as those changes carry readiness conditions.
Does not apply to catalogue expansion, pricing changes or routine operational changes on an already-active account.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Activation
The point at which a seller's listings become buyable
Readiness condition
A verifiable condition attached to a commercial entitlement
Milestone
A readiness condition with a defined validator and date
Compensating control
A measure that bounds risk where a condition is unmet
Policy exception
A documented, time-bound departure from a stated condition
Closure standard
The evidence required to consider a condition satisfied
Two-stage onboarding
Activation on an interim process with a committed migration
4. Activation Conditions
A seller may not be activated unless all of the following are satisfied.

"},{"evidence_id":"EV-2f8d187c53fc","text":"R-5. Any settlement dispute resets W-1 to zero.
The seller portal describes weekly settlement as a tier feature without stating these conditions. That discrepancy was raised in January 2026 and is a known documentation gap on the seller-facing side. Until it is corrected, account managers should state the conditions explicitly when a seller raises the subject.
5.2 Tier Upgrade
R-6. Tier is reviewed annually, or on milestone completion where a conditional upgrade is in effect.
R-7. Tier may be reviewed downward where order defect rate exceeds the tier threshold for two consecutive months.
R-8. Tier and settlement frequency are separable. A tier upgrade may be granted where a settlement frequency change may not, because the two carry different and asymmetric risks: a tier change is commercially reversible at the next review, whereas settlement frequency determines how much unreconciled value is paid out before a dispute could surface.
6. Closure Standard
R-9. A condition is satisfied by evidence that the thing works, not by evidence that it has been configured.
Condition type
Acceptable evidence
Failover configuration
A successful live failover test
Monitoring or alerting
The alert observed firing in a controlled test
Data quality rule
A rejection report showing the rule acting
Interim process removal
The interim process confirmed retired
Seller-side capability
Confirmation from the named seller counterpart
Reconciliation capability
A reconciliation run compared against platform figures
R-10. A configuration entry, a ticket marked complete, or a verbal assurance is not acceptable closure evidence for any condition in section 4 or 5.
Rule R-9 was added in July 2026. A failover condition had been closed in October 2025 on a configuration entry; when the failover was required eight months later, the stored credentials had expired and no label could be generated for 2,100 perishable orders. The condition had been recorded as met and had never been true.
7. Exceptions
R-11. An exception to any condition in sections 4 or 5 requires all of the following:
1. A written rationale stating what is being waived and why.
2. A named approver with authority for the affected domain.
3. A compensating control that bounds the resulting risk.
4. Milestones with named validators where the condition is deferred rather than waived.
5. An expiry date, after which the exception lapses and the entitlement is withdrawn.

"},{"evidence_id":"EV-e818fdac7226","text":"R-12. An exception may not waive A-2 (KYC), A-3 (category compliance) or A-9 (tax mapping). These are compliance conditions, not commercial ones.
R-13. Two-stage onboarding is permitted where an interim process is used at activation, provided the exception carries an explicit exit date. An open-ended commitment to migrate is not an acceptable exception; in practice it becomes permanent.
R-14. A compensating control must be proportionate to the exposure it bounds, and must be sized against the risk rather than against the seller's convenience. A security deposit, for example, is sized against the largest single-cycle dispute observed on comparable accounts.
R-15. Every active exception is reviewed at each quarterly account review.
7.1 Worked Example
A grocery seller requested a tier upgrade and weekly settlement in January 2026, having completed four settlement cycles, with no automated reconciliation and an untested failover.
The tier upgrade was granted immediately, because tier risk is commercially reversible. Weekly settlement was deferred and tied to validation of the reconciliation milestone, with a security deposit as the compensating control and an expiry date of 31 January 2027.
Three of four milestones were subsequently met. The reconciliation milestone remains outstanding as of
September 2026, and weekly settlement has accordingly not been granted. The exception is operating as intended: the commercial benefit was delivered where it was safe to do so, and the financial control held.

During a BluePeak flash sale, order placement latency rose to a p99 of 12.4 seconds and 3,900 order placements failed with HTTP 503 over approximately 40 minutes. The order service connection pool was exhausted by an amplified retry load, worsened by the absence of a circuit breaker on a slow downstream inventory lookup.

This was classified SEV-1 rather than SEV-2 because the shared order placement path was degraded for all sellers, not only for the seller whose traffic triggered it.
3. Detection
Detected by the seller during the live event.
BluePeak's integration lead called Support at 20:07 IST, seven minutes after the sale opened, reporting that roughly one in three order placements was failing. Support confirmed from platform metrics and escalated at
20:12.
Platform latency alerts did fire, at 20:09, two minutes before escalation. The alert reached the on-call channel but the seller call had already started by then. In practice the seller and the alert detected the problem at effectively the same time, which is a poor outcome for a SEV-1 on a pre-announced event.

5. Symptoms
 HTTP 503 responses from the order placement endpoint.
 p99 latency rising steadily rather than spiking, over roughly four minutes.
 Connection pool utilisation pinned at 100 percent.
 Inventory lookup dependency responding slowly but not failing.
 Total inbound request volume far exceeding the expected traffic profile for the announced sale size.
 CPU and memory on order service instances well within normal range.
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL
INC-2026-0716 | Incident Report
Page 2 of 5

The last symptom was important. The service was not resource-constrained. It was blocked, waiting on connections held by requests waiting on a slow dependency.
6. Affected Services
Service
Role
State
Order Service
Order placement
Degraded: pool exhausted
API gateway
Request ingress
Functioning; no load shedding
configured
Inventory lookup service

Slow, not failed

Unaffected
BluePeak client
Order placement caller
Amplifying load through unbounded
retries
7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.
9. Contributing Factors
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL
INC-2026-0716 | Incident Report
Page 3 of 5

1. No circuit breaker on a synchronous dependency in the critical path.
2. No connection acquisition timeout, so requests queued instead of failing fast.
3. Unbounded client retries at the seller, with no backoff or jitter.
4. HTTP 503 as the overload response, which does not communicate a retry strategy. A 429 with Retry-After states the correct behaviour explicitly.
5. No advance notice of the sale. The platform learned of the event when the traffic arrived. No capacity assessment was possible.
6. Pool sized for steady state, never load-tested against a dependency degradation scenario.
10. Mitigation
Two actions restored service.
The emergency pool increase from 120 to 240 at 20:26 bought immediate headroom and reduced the error rate from 31 percent to approximately 10 percent within 12 minutes. This treated the symptom.
Rate limiting the highest-volume client at 20:31 addressed the amplification and took the error rate below 2
percent by 20:44. This was the action that actually ended the incident, and it is uncomfortable: the platform throttled a seller's traffic during that seller's own revenue event. It was the correct call, because the throttled traffic was overwhelmingly retries rather than genuine buyer demand.
Time from escalation to mitigation: 32 minutes.
11. Resolution
Permanent remediation was delivered under the S002 throughput and resilience programme, workstream
WS-A, on 26 August 2026:
 Circuit breaker on the inventory lookup, opening at a 25 percent error rate over a 10-second window with a 30-second half-open probe.
 Connection pool resized to 300 with an explicit acquisition timeout of
750 ms, so a saturated pool fails fast.
 Request-level timeout of 2.5 seconds on the order placement path, replacing
10 seconds.
 Overload responses changed from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with Retry-After.
BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.

7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.

At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.

Two actions restored service.
The emergency pool increase from 120 to 240 at 20:26 bought immediate headroom and reduced the error rate from 31 percent to approximately 10 percent within 12 minutes. This treated the symptom.
Rate limiting the highest-volume client at 20:31 addressed the amplification and took the error rate below 2

WS-A, on 26 August 2026:

10 seconds.

BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.

evidence.answer_quote: **Next steps after the outage**

- **Review the post‑incident actions**  
  - The incident was closed with a set of permanent remediation items (circuit breaker on the inventory lookup, pool resize with acquisition timeout, overload response change to HTTP 429, etc.). Verify that all of these items are now in production for your account.

- **Validate the preventive actions**  
  - Confirm that the following actions are marked **Complete** for your seller (S002 – BluePeak Electronics):  
    - PA‑1: Circuit breaker on inventory lookup  
    - PA‑2: Pool resize and acquisition timeout  
    - PA‑3: HTTP 429 with Retry‑After for overload  
    - PA‑4: Requirement NFR‑5 – graceful load shedding  
    - PA‑5: 10‑working‑day capacity notice (now contractual)

- **Track in‑progress items**  
  - Ensure the following work items are progressing as planned:  
    - PA‑6: Capacity model for declared sale profiles (target 2026‑10‑09)  
    - PA‑7: Client‑side retry hardening at BluePeak (target 2026‑10‑23) – not started yet  
    - PA‑8: Dependency‑degradation load test in the release pipeline (target 2026‑11‑20)

- **Run validation tests**  
  - Perform the synthetic storm test (4× July peak) to confirm that the pool no longer exhausts and that overload responses are now HTTP 429.  
  - Verify that the new request‑level timeout (2.5 s) and acquisition timeout (750 ms) are effective under load.

- **Update operational monitoring**  
  - Ensure latency alerts fire early enough (they previously fired at 20:09, two minutes before escalation).  
  - Add monitoring for connection‑pool utilisation and retry‑storm metrics to catch similar patterns early.

- **Coordinate with the seller**  
  - Work with BluePeak’s integration lead to implement the client‑side changes (bounded retries with exponential backoff, jitter, and a client‑side circuit breaker) scheduled for the October release train.

- **Document the follow‑up**  
  - Record the review outcomes, any remaining open items, and the timeline for completion in a post‑incident follow‑up document. This will serve as the reference for future flash‑sale events.

Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. 7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.

Two actions restored service.

10 seconds.

BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.

During a BluePeak flash sale, order placement latency rose to a p99 of 12.4 seconds and 3,900 order placements failed with HTTP 503 over approximately 40 minutes. The order service connection pool was exhausted by an amplified retry load, worsened by the absence of a circuit breaker on a slow downstream inventory lookup.

Page 1 of 5

This was classified SEV-1 rather than SEV-2 because the shared order placement path was degraded for all sellers, not only for the seller whose traffic triggered it.
3. Detection
Detected by the seller during the live event.
BluePeak's integration lead called Support at 20:07 IST, seven minutes after the sale opened, reporting that roughly one in three order placements was failing. Support confirmed from platform metrics and escalated at
20:12.
Platform latency alerts did fire, at 20:09, two minutes before escalation. The alert reached the on-call channel but the seller call had already started by then. In practice the seller and the alert detected the problem at effectively the same time, which is a poor outcome for a SEV-1 on a pre-announced event.

5. Symptoms
 HTTP 503 responses from the order placement endpoint.
 p99 latency rising steadily rather than spiking, over roughly four minutes.
 Connection pool utilisation pinned at 100 percent.
 Inventory lookup dependency responding slowly but not failing.
 Total inbound request volume far exceeding the expected traffic profile for the announced sale size.
 CPU and memory on order service instances well within normal range.
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL
INC-2026-0716 | Incident Report
Page 2 of 5

The last symptom was important. The service was not resource-constrained. It was blocked, waiting on connections held by requests waiting on a slow dependency.
6. Affected Services
Service
Role
State
Order Service
Order placement
Degraded: pool exhausted
API gateway
Request ingress
Functioning; no load shedding
configured
Inventory lookup service

Slow, not failed

Cart retrieval
Unaffected
BluePeak client
Order placement caller
Amplifying load through unbounded
retries
7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.
9. Contributing Factors
Nexora Commerce Pvt. Ltd. | Nexora Marketplace
CLASSIFICATION: CONFIDENTIAL
INC-2026-0716 | Incident Report
Page 3 of 5

1. No circuit breaker on a synchronous dependency in the critical path.
2. No connection acquisition timeout, so requests queued instead of failing fast.
3. Unbounded client retries at the seller, with no backoff or jitter.
4. HTTP 503 as the overload response, which does not communicate a retry strategy. A 429 with Retry-After states the correct behaviour explicitly.
5. No advance notice of the sale. The platform learned of the event when the traffic arrived. No capacity assessment was possible.
6. Pool sized for steady state, never load-tested against a dependency degradation scenario.
10. Mitigation
Two actions restored service.
The emergency pool increase from 120 to 240 at 20:26 bought immediate headroom and reduced the error rate from 31 percent to approximately 10 percent within 12 minutes. This treated the symptom.
Rate limiting the highest-volume client at 20:31 addressed the amplification and took the error rate below 2
percent by 20:44. This was the action that actually ended the incident, and it is uncomfortable: the platform throttled a seller's traffic during that seller's own revenue event. It was the correct call, because the throttled traffic was overwhelmingly retries rather than genuine buyer demand.
Time from escalation to mitigation: 32 minutes.
11. Resolution
Permanent remediation was delivered under the S002 throughput and resilience programme, workstream
WS-A, on 26 August 2026:
 Circuit breaker on the inventory lookup, opening at a 25 percent error rate over a 10-second window with a 30-second half-open probe.
 Connection pool resized to 300 with an explicit acquisition timeout of
750 ms, so a saturated pool fails fast.
 Request-level timeout of 2.5 seconds on the order placement path, replacing
10 seconds.
 Overload responses changed from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with Retry-After.
BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.

"},{"evidence_id":"EV-30ab7c5a377b","text":"This was classified SEV-1 rather than SEV-2 because the shared order placement path was degraded for all sellers, not only for the seller whose traffic triggered it.
3. Detection
Detected by the seller during the live event.
BluePeak's integration lead called Support at 20:07 IST, seven minutes after the sale opened, reporting that roughly one in three order placements was failing. Support confirmed from platform metrics and escalated at
20:12.
Platform latency alerts did fire, at 20:09, two minutes before escalation. The alert reached the on-call channel but the seller call had already started by then. In practice the seller and the alert detected the problem at effectively the same time, which is a poor outcome for a SEV-1 on a pre-announced event.

"},{"evidence_id":"EV-1b9d2f245c22","text":"The last symptom was important. The service was not resource-constrained. It was blocked, waiting on connections held by requests waiting on a slow dependency.
6. Affected Services
Service
Role
State
Order Service
Order placement
Degraded: pool exhausted
API gateway

configured
Inventory lookup service
Availability check during placement
Slow, not failed
Cart service
Cart retrieval
Unaffected
BluePeak client
Order placement caller
Amplifying load through unbounded
retries
7. Investigation
7.1 The Proximate Cause
Order placement calls the inventory lookup service synchronously. Under normal load that call returns in about 40 ms. Under flash-sale load it slowed to 600-900 ms, because the lookup fans out across a much larger set of SKUs than a typical order.
Each in-flight placement holds a connection from a fixed pool of 120 for the duration of that call. At 9x baseline traffic with a 15x slower dependency, demand for connections exceeded 120 within about four minutes. Once the pool was full, new requests queued with no acquisition timeout and eventually returned
503.
7.2 The Amplification
The failure would have been self-limiting if clients had backed off. They did not.
BluePeak's client retried timed-out placements without limit and without backoff. Every 503 produced another request. Measured inbound volume at 20:18 was approximately 3.4 times the volume implied by actual buyer activity, so roughly 70 percent of the traffic at peak was retries of already-failed requests.
This is why no static capacity figure would have been sufficient. An unbounded retry loop expands to consume whatever capacity exists.
7.3 The Missing Control
The inventory lookup had no circuit breaker. A slow dependency should eventually be bypassed or failed fast, so that callers release their connections. Instead, every caller waited the full timeout, and the timeout on that path was 10 seconds.
A 10-second timeout with a 120-connection pool caps throughput at 12 requests per second once the dependency is slow, regardless of how much capacity the service otherwise has.
8. Root Cause
The order service connection pool was exhausted because synchronous inventory lookups slowed under flash-sale load and were not protected by a circuit breaker or an acquisition timeout, while an unbounded client retry policy amplified inbound traffic to roughly 3.4 times genuine demand. The combination converted a capacity pressure into a 40-minute cascading failure.
9. Contributing Factors

"},{"evidence_id":"EV-cd9caad63986","text":"1. No circuit breaker on a synchronous dependency in the critical path.
2. No connection acquisition timeout, so requests queued instead of failing fast.
3. Unbounded client retries at the seller, with no backoff or jitter.
4. HTTP 503 as the overload response, which does not communicate a retry strategy. A 429 with Retry-After states the correct behaviour explicitly.
5. No advance notice of the sale. The platform learned of the event when the traffic arrived. No capacity assessment was possible.
6. Pool sized for steady state, never load-tested against a dependency degradation scenario.
10. Mitigation
Two actions restored service.
The emergency pool increase from 120 to 240 at 20:26 bought immediate headroom and reduced the error rate from 31 percent to approximately 10 percent within 12 minutes. This treated the symptom.
Rate limiting the highest-volume client at 20:31 addressed the amplification and took the error rate below 2
percent by 20:44. This was the action that actually ended the incident, and it is uncomfortable: the platform throttled a seller's traffic during that seller's own revenue event. It was the correct call, because the throttled traffic was overwhelmingly retries rather than genuine buyer demand.
Time from escalation to mitigation: 32 minutes.
11. Resolution
Permanent remediation was delivered under the S002 throughput and resilience programme, workstream
WS-A, on 26 August 2026:
 Circuit breaker on the inventory lookup, opening at a 25 percent error rate over a 10-second window with a 30-second half-open probe.
 Connection pool resized to 300 with an explicit acquisition timeout of
750 ms, so a saturated pool fails fast.
 Request-level timeout of 2.5 seconds on the order placement path, replacing
10 seconds.
 Overload responses changed from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with Retry-After.
BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.

- **Update operational monitoring**  
  - Ensure latency alerts fire early enough (they previously fired at 20:09, two minutes before escalation).

WS-A, on 26 August 2026:

 Connection pool resized to 300 with an explicit acquisition timeout of
750 ms, so a saturated pool fails fast.
 Request-level timeout of 2.5 seconds on the order placement path, replacing
10 seconds.
 Overload responses changed from HTTP 503 to HTTP 429 with Retry-After.
BluePeak owns the client-side changes: bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring
Retry-After, and a client-side circuit breaker. Those are scheduled in the seller's October release train.
